blocks.text: Calling `push` O(1) can feel like cheating, since some pushes copy the entire array. Amortised analysis is the tool that makes the claim precise — and it applies to several patterns you have already met.
An **amortised** cost is the average cost per operation across a worst-case *sequence*, not the worst case of a single operation.

This is stronger than an average over random inputs. There is no probability involved: the guarantee is that **any** sequence of N pushes costs O(N) in total, so no adversary can construct a bad case.
Push N elements, starting from capacity 1. The cheap work is N writes. The expensive work is the copying at each resize:

blocks.code:
copies  =  1 + 2 + 4 + ... + N/2 + N   <   2N

total   =  N writes  +  <2N copies   =   <3N operations
per push = 3N / N = 3 = O(1)

blocks.text: A constant, independent of N. That is the whole argument.
An alternative framing many find more intuitive. Charge every push **three** tokens instead of one:

items: One pays for writing the new element.
One is saved to pay for copying this element later.
One is saved to pay for copying an older element that has already spent its savings.

blocks.text: When a resize happens, the elements being copied have collectively saved exactly enough to pay for it. The bank balance never goes negative — so a constant charge per push covers everything, forever.
An **individual** push can still be O(N), and occasionally will be. Amortised analysis bounds the total, not the maximum.

That distinction matters for real-time systems — audio processing, game frame loops — where a single unexpected pause is unacceptable even if the average is fine. Those systems preallocate capacity precisely to avoid the spike.
Where else you have seen this
The same reasoning justified two earlier patterns:

items: **Sliding window** — the inner `while` looks nested, but `left` advances at most N times overall.
**Longest consecutive sequence** — the inner walk seems quadratic, but each element is walked exactly once across the whole run.

blocks.text: Recognising amortised behaviour is what lets you tell a genuinely quadratic loop from one that merely looks it.
